claim: The human cerebral cortex is symmetrically organized along large-scale axes but also presents inter-hemispheric differences in structure and function.
source: The human cerebral cortex is symmetrically organized along large-scale axes but also presents inter-hemispheric differences in structure and function.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by citations throughout the manuscript to prior work.

claim: Asymmetry is a key feature of the human brain left-right axis supporting functional processes, such as language.
source: The quantified contralateral homologous difference, that is asymmetry, is a key feature of the human brain left-right axis supporting functional processes, such as language.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the introduction.

claim: The asymmetry of cortical functional organization is heritable in humans.
source: Our findings indicate asymmetric organization along an axis describing a functional trajectory from perceptual/action to abstract cognition. Whereas language network showed leftward asymmetric organization, frontoparietal network showed rightward asymmetric organization in humans. These asymmetries were heritable in humans
evidence: This claim is supported by heritability analyses presented in Figure 3 and associated text.

claim: Language network showed leftward asymmetric organization in humans.
source: Whereas language network showed leftward asymmetric organization, frontoparietal network showed rightward asymmetric organization in humans.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2c and associated statistical analyses.

claim: Frontoparietal network showed rightward asymmetric organization in humans.
source: Whereas language network showed leftward asymmetric organization, frontoparietal network showed rightward asymmetric organization in humans.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2c and associated statistical analyses.

claim: Asymmetries in functional organization showed a similar spatial distribution between humans and macaques in the case of intra-hemispheric asymmetry of functional hierarchy.
source: These asymmetries were heritable in humans and showed a similar spatial distribution with macaques, in the case of intra-hemispheric asymmetry of functional hierarchy.
evidence: This is supported by cross-species comparison data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Both language and frontoparietal networks showed a qualitatively larger asymmetry in humans relative to macaques.
source: However, both language and frontoparietal networks showed a qualitatively larger asymmetry in humans relative to macaques.
evidence: This is supported by comparative data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Asymmetry in intrinsic functional organization has a genetic basis.
source: Overall, our findings suggest a genetic basis for asymmetry in intrinsic functional organization, linked to higher order cognitive functions uniquely developed in humans.
evidence: This is inferred from the heritability analyses and cross-species comparisons presented in the study.

claim: The brain favors asymmetry to avoid duplication of neural circuitry having equivalent functions.
source: It has been suggested that the brain favors asymmetry to avoid duplication of neural circuitry having equivalent functions (Karolis et al., 2019; Levy, 1977).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Bilateral cortical regions showing asymmetry in task-evoked activity have reduced long-range connections with the opposite homologous regions, favoring more local connectivity.
source: For example, bilateral cortical regions showing asymmetry in task-evoked activity have reduced (long-range) connections with the opposite homologous regions, favoring more local connectivity (Karolis et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Functions related to leftward dominance include language processing.
source: Previous work has suggested that functions related to leftward dominance include language processing (Lane et al., 2017; Piervincenzi et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2019), letter search (Pollack and Price, 2019), and analogical reasoning (Urbanski et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Rightward dominance of functional activation has been related to visuospatial abilities.
source: On the other hand, rightward dominance of functional activation has been related to holistic word processing (Ventura et al., 2019), visuospatial abilities (Chen et al., 2019), emotional processing (Moeck et al., 2020), as well as with psychiatric disorders such as autism spectrum disorder (Floris et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Language areas of the middle and superior temporal cortex showed increased connectivity with regions in the left hemisphere relative to their right hemispheric counterparts.
source: For example, language areas of the middle and superior temporal cortex showed increased connectivity with regions in the left hemisphere relative to their right hemispheric counterparts (Raemaekers et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The right amygdala showed higher connectivity with the entire cortex than the left amygdala.
source: and the right amygdala showed higher connectivity with the entire cortex than the left amygdala (Tetereva et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: There are inter- and intra-hemispheric differences in functional connectivity between healthy adults and patients with schizophrenia.
source: Moreover, previous work has indicated that there are inter- and intra-hemispheric differences in functional connectivity between healthy adults and patients with schizophrenia (Agcaoglu et al., 2018), and between neurotypical individuals and those diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (Hahamy et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Functional processing asymmetries may be driven by subtle differences in functional organization between the hemispheres.
source: It is possible that such functional processing asymmetries may be driven by subtle differences in functional organization between the hemispheres.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from prior observations.

claim: Gradients capture how connectivity profiles from distinct cortical regions are integrated and segregated across the cortex.
source: Gradients capture how connectivity profiles from distinct cortical regions are integrated (i.e. similar functional connectivity profiles) and segregated (i.e. dissimilar functional connectivity profiles) across the cortex (Margulies et al., 2016; Bethlehem et al., 2020; Haak and Beckmann, 2020; Paquola et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The principal functional gradient shows that regions of the transmodal systems occupy locations equidistant from unimodal systems.
source: The principal functional gradient, partly reflected in the intrinsic geometry of the cortex, shows that regions of the transmodal systems occupy locations equidistant from unimodal systems (Margulies et al., 2016; Hong et al., 2020; Murphy et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Gradients describe variations in genetic patterning.
source: They describe variations in genetic patterning (Vainik et al., 2020; Valk et al., 2020; Valk et al., 2022, functional processes Margulies et al., 2016; Murphy et al., 2018; Turnbull et al., 2020), and are observed across species (Valk et al., 2020; Coletta et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Gradients are observed across species.
source: They describe variations in genetic patterning (Vainik et al., 2020; Valk et al., 2020; Valk et al., 2022, functional processes Margulies et al., 2016; Murphy et al., 2018; Turnbull et al., 2020), and are observed across species (Valk et al., 2020; Coletta et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The principal gradient describes the geodesic distance between primary and default regions.
source: Moreover, the principal gradient describes the geodesic distance between primary and default regions, and relates to cortical microstructure and associated processing hierarchies (Huntenburg et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The principal gradient is asymmetric.
source: Indeed, recent research suggests that the principal gradient is asymmetric (Liang et al., 2021; Gonzalez Alam et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The degree of asymmetry relates to individual differences in semantic performance and visual reasoning.
source: and that the degree of asymmetry relates to individual differences in semantic performance and visual reasoning (Gonzalez Alam et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: There may be important (phylo)genetic factors supporting lateralized human cognition.
source: As inter-hemispheric asymmetry has been observed consistently in human brain structure and function, there may be important (phylo)genetic factors supporting lateralized human cognition (Güntürkün et al., 2020; Corballis, 1989; Corballis, 2009; Güntürkün and Ocklenburg, 2017; Vilain et al., 2011; Vallortigara et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and represents an inference from observed patterns.

claim: Brain structure asymmetry is heritable, especially in the language areas.
source: Previous work has reported that brain structure asymmetry is heritable (Sha et al., 2021; Zhong et al., 2021), especially in the language areas, and differentiates between humans and non-human primates (Eichert et al., 2020; Eichert et al., 2019; Neubauer et al., 2020; Spocter et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Both humans and apes show asymmetry of brain shape.
source: At the same time, it has been shown that both humans and apes show asymmetry of brain shape (Neubauer et al., 2020), indicating that asymmetry is not a uniquely human brain feature.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Intra-hemispheric connections have been suggested to reflect inhibition of the corpus callosum and may underlie hemispheric specializations involving language, reasoning, and attention.
source: Intra-hemispheric connections, compared to the inter-hemispheric connections, have been suggested to reflect inhibition of the corpus callosum and may underlie hemispheric specializations involving language, reasoning, and attention (Gazzaniga, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Inter-hemispheric connectivity may reflect information transfer between hemispheres.
source: Conversely, inter-hemispheric connectivity may reflect information transfer between hemispheres, for example, of motoric information, or crude information concerning spatial locations (Gazzaniga, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Inter-hemispheric connectivity has been reported to be abnormal in patients with schizophrenia.
source: For example, inter-hemispheric connectivity has been reported to be abnormal in patients with schizophrenia (Agcaoglu et al., 2018; Chang et al., 2019) and autism (Hahamy et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The first three FC LL gradients explained 24.1%, 18.4%, and 15.1% of total variance in humans.
source: Each gradient has reasonably well-described functional associations (G1: unimodal-transmodal gradient with 24.1%, G2: somatosensory-visual gradient with 18.4%, G3: multi-demand gradient with 15.1%).
evidence: This is directly reported from the data analysis.

claim: The individual mean gradients showed high correlation with the group gradients LL (all Spearman r>0.97, P spin <0.001).
source: The individual mean gradients showed high correlation with the group gradients LL (all Spearman r>0.97, P spin <0.001).
evidence: This is directly reported from the statistical analysis.

claim: For the intra-hemispheric pattern, the mean gradients of LL were strongly correlated with those of RR (Spearman rG1=0.988, Pspin <0.001, rG2=0.989, Pspin <0.001, rG3=0.967, Pspin <0.001).
source: For the intra-hemispheric pattern, the mean gradients of LL were strongly correlated with those of RR (Spearman rG1=0.988, Pspin <0.001, rG2=0.989, Pspin <0.001, rG3=0.967, Pspin <0.001).
evidence: This is directly reported from the statistical analysis.

claim: For the inter-hemispheric pattern, the mean gradients of LR were strongly correlated with those of RL (Spearman rG1=0.993, Pspin <0.001, rG2=0.985, Pspin <0.001, rG3=0.969, Pspin <0.001).
source: For the inter-hemispheric pattern, the mean gradients of LR were also strongly correlated with those of RL (Spearman rG1=0.993, Pspin <0.001, rG2=0.985, Pspin <0.001, rG3=0.969, Pspin <0.001).
evidence: This is directly reported from the statistical analysis.

claim: The principal gradient (G1) traversed between unimodal regions and transmodal regions.
source: Similar to previous work (Coifman et al., 2005) we observed that the principal gradient (G1) traversed between unimodal regions and transmodal regions (e.g. default-mode network: DMN)
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1d and comparison to prior work.

claim: A visual to somatosensory gradient was found for G2.
source: whereas a visual to somatosensory gradient was found for G2.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The tertiary gradient (G3) dissociated control from DMN and sensory-motor networks.
source: The tertiary gradient (G3) dissociated control from DMN and sensory-motor networks (Figure 1d and e, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Frontal and temporal lobes showed the greatest intra-hemispheric asymmetry in G1.
source: Frontal and temporal lobes showed the greatest intra-hemispheric asymmetry in G1 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis results.

claim: Regions in ventral- and dorsolateral PFC (11 l, p9-46v, p10p) were the three most rightward asymmetric areas in the intra-hemispheric pattern.
source: In particular, regions in ventral- and dorsolateral PFC (11 l, p9-46v, p10p) were the three most rightward asymmetric areas
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis results shown in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Regions in temporal polar cortex, dorso/posterior superior temporal sulcus, and inferior frontal gyrus (TGv, STSdp, and 55b) were the three most leftward asymmetric areas in the intra-hemispheric pattern.
source: and regions in temporal polar cortex, dorso/posterior superior temporal sulcus, and inferior frontal gyrus (TGv, STSdp, and 55b) were the three most leftward asymmetric areas in the intra-hemispheric pattern.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis results shown in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The language network had a high leftward AI (t=41.3, df = 1013, P FDR < 0.001).
source: Network-level analyses (Figure 2c) indicated that the language (t=41.3, df = 1013, P FDR < 0.001) and default mode (t=17.3, df = 1013, P FDR < 0.001) networks had a high leftward AI
evidence: This is directly reported from the statistical analysis.

claim: The default mode network had a high leftward AI (t=17.3, df = 1013, P FDR < 0.001).
source: Network-level analyses (Figure 2c) indicated that the language (t=41.3, df = 1013, P FDR < 0.001) and default mode (t=17.3, df = 1013, P FDR < 0.001) networks had a high leftward AI
evidence: This is directly reported from the statistical analysis.

claim: The frontoparietal network had a high rightward AI (t=–26.0, df = 1013, P FDR < 0.001).
source: while the frontoparietal network (t=–26.0, df = 1013, P FDR < 0.001) had a high rightward AI.
evidence: This is directly reported from the statistical analysis.

claim: No significant difference of AI was observed in primary and secondary visual networks.
source: We observed no significant difference of AI in primary and secondary visual networks.
evidence: This is directly reported from the statistical analysis.

claim: The mean AI scores across individuals for the intra- and inter-hemispheric patterns showed high similarity (Spearman r G1 = 0.645, P spin <0.001).
source: The mean AI scores across individuals for the intra- and inter-hemispheric patterns showed high similarity (Spearman r G1 = 0.645, P spin <0.001).
evidence: This is directly reported from the statistical analysis.

claim: Left-right differences observed in large-scale functional organization axes were heritable.
source: We found that left-right differences observed in large-scale functional organization axes were heritable (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by heritability analysis results shown in Figure 3a.

claim: For the intra-hemispheric pattern, sensory-motor regions, middle temporal regions, dorso-lateral, and medial prefrontal regions were heritable (P FDR < 0.05).
source: Specifically, for the intra-hemispheric pattern, we found sensory-motor regions, middle temporal regions, dorso-lateral, and medial prefrontal regions to be heritable (P FDR < 0.05).
evidence: This is directly reported from the heritability analysis.

claim: For the inter-hemispheric pattern, all cortical regions with the exception of visual areas and superior temporal and insular regions were heritable (P FDR < 0.05).
source: In the case of the inter-hemispheric pattern, all cortical regions with the exception of visual areas and superior temporal and insular regions were heritable (P FDR < 0.05).
evidence: This is directly reported from the heritability analysis.

claim: Language-associated areas such as the PSL (Peri-Sylvian language area) and 55b had the highest heritability in both the hemispheric patterns.
source: Notably, language-associated areas such as the PSL (Peri-Sylvian language area) and 55b had the highest heritability in both the hemispheric patterns (PSL: intra: h2=0.46, P FDR < 0.001 and inter: h2=0.34, P FDR < 0.001, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is directly reported from the heritability analysis.

claim: BA area 44 (Broca's area) showed low heritability (intra: h2 = 0.12, P FDR = 0.026 and inter: h2=0.12, P FDR = 0.018).
source: However, BA area 44 (Broca's area) showed low heritability (intra: hGüntürkün et al., 2020 = 0.12, P FDR = 0.026 and inter: h2=0.12, P FDR = 0.018).
evidence: This is directly reported from the heritability analysis.

claim: For the intra-hemispheric FC patterns, gradients showed significant correlation between absolute asymmetry index and heritability (Pearson r=0.245, P spin = 0.005).
source: For the correlation between the absolute asymmetry index and heritability (Figure 3b small scatter), gradients of the intra-hemispheric FC patterns were significant (Pearson r=0.245, P spin = 0.005)
evidence: This is directly reported from the statistical analysis.

claim: For the inter-hemispheric FC patterns, gradients showed no significant correlation between absolute asymmetry index and heritability (Pearson r=0.055, P spin = 0.613).
source: while gradients of the inter-hemispheric FC were not (Pearson r=0.055, P spin = 0.613).
evidence: This is directly reported from the statistical analysis.

claim: The first three template gradients in macaques explained 20.0%, 15.2%, and 12.8% of total variance, respectively.
source: The first three template gradients explained 20.0%, 15.2%, and 12.8% of total variance, respectively.
evidence: This is directly reported from the data analysis of macaque data.

claim: G1 in macaques described an axis traversing dorsolateral prefrontal and parietal regions (anterior-posterior).
source: G1 described an axis traversing dorsolateral prefrontal and parietal regions (anterior-posterior).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: In macaques, parietal cortices had a rightward dominance while occipital cortices were leftward along G1 of the intra-hemispheric pattern.
source: Evaluating the intra-hemispheric pattern of functional organization in macaques along G1, we observed that parietal cortices had a rightward dominance while occipital cortices were leftward.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The AI scores of the principal, secondary and tertiary gradients in macaques were not statistically significant after FDR correction, both for intra- and inter-hemispheric patterns.
source: However, the AI scores of the principal, but also secondary and tertiary gradients, were not statistically significant after FDR correction, both for intra- and inter-hemispheric patterns.
evidence: This is directly reported from the statistical analysis.

claim: The macaque and macaque-aligned human AI maps of G1 were correlated positively for intra-hemispheric patterns (Pearson r=0.345, P spin = 0.030).
source: We found that the macaque and macaque-aligned human AI maps of G1 were correlated positively for intra-hemispheric patterns (Pearson r=0.345, P spin = 0.030).
evidence: This is directly reported from the cross-species comparison analysis.

claim: For inter-hemispheric patterns, no significant association was observed between macaque and human AI maps (Pearson r=–0.029, P spin = 0.858).
source: For inter-hemispheric patterns, we did not observe a significant association (Pearson r=–0.029, P spin = 0.858).
evidence: This is directly reported from the cross-species comparison analysis.

claim: Humans showed high leftward asymmetry in the language and default mode networks but macaques did not.
source: In the case of the intra-hemispheric asymmetry of the principal FC gradient, we observed that humans showed high leftward asymmetry in the language and default mode networks but macaques did not.
evidence: This is supported by the comparative data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Humans showed high rightward asymmetry in the frontoparietal and cingulo-opercular networks but macaques did not.
source: Moreover, humans showed high rightward asymmetry in the frontoparietal and cingulo-opercular networks but macaques did not.
evidence: This is supported by the comparative data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Humans and macaques showed an opposite direction of asymmetry in auditory, orbito-affective, and secondary visual networks.
source: Humans and macaques showed an opposite direction of asymmetry in auditory, orbito-affective, and secondary visual networks.
evidence: This is supported by the comparative data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Language, semantics, and reading domains were associated with leftward hemispheric preference.
source: Language, semantics, and reading domains were associated with leftward hemispheric preference, whereas cognitive control, inhibition, and working memory were associated with rightward hemispheric preference.
evidence: This is supported by the functional decoding analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Cognitive control, inhibition, and working memory were associated with rightward hemispheric preference.
source: Language, semantics, and reading domains were associated with leftward hemispheric preference, whereas cognitive control, inhibition, and working memory were associated with rightward hemispheric preference.
evidence: This is supported by the functional decoding analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Patterns of asymmetry in functional organization align with task-based activations consistently reported in the literature.
source: This indicates that patterns of asymmetry in functional organization also align with task-based activations consistently reported in the literature.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional decoding analysis results.

claim: For G1, asymmetric effects using AI_norm were highly correlated with the main asymmetric effects (Spearman r intra- hemisphere = 0.851, P uncorrected <0.001; r inter-hemisphere = 0.863, P uncorrected <0.001).
source: We found that for G1, asymmetric effects were highly correlated with the main asymmetric effects (Spearman r intra- hemisphere = 0.851, P uncorrected <0.001; r inter-hemisphere = 0.863, P uncorrected <0.001).
evidence: This is directly reported from the robustness analysis.

claim: A high correlation was observed between the LL functional gradient between HCP and UKB (Spearman r G1 = -0.588, P uncorrected <0.001; Spearman r G2 = 0.309, P uncorrected <0.001; Spearman r G3 = 0.773, P uncorrected <0.001).
source: We observed a high correlation between the LL functional gradient between HCP and UKB (Spearman r G1 = -0.588, P uncorrected <0.001; Spearman r G2 = 0.309, P uncorrected <0.001; Spearman r G3 = 0.773, P uncorrected <0.001).
evidence: This is directly reported from the replication analysis using UKB data.

claim: For the G1 of the intra-hemispheric FC pattern in UKB, a correlation was observed with findings in the HCP sample (Pearson r intra-hemisphere = 0.592, P spin <0.001; Pearson r inter-hemisphere = 0.384, P spin <0.001).
source: For the G1 of the intra-hemispheric FC pattern, we observed a correlation with our findings in the HCP sample (Pearson r intra-hemisphere = 0.592, P spin <0.001; Pearson r inter-hemisphere = 0.384, P spin <0.001).
evidence: This is directly reported from the replication analysis using UKB data.

claim: In UKB, language and default mode networks showed leftward asymmetry, but the frontoparietal network did not show rightward asymmetry.
source: However, we found that language and default mode networks showed leftward asymmetry (as in HCP), but the frontoparietal network did not show rightward asymmetry.
evidence: This is directly reported from the replication analysis using UKB data.

claim: Comparing gradient asymmetry with Procrustes alignment to gradient without alignment resulted in virtually identical results for the HCP sample (r intra-hemisphere = 0.956, r inter-hemisphere = 0.843).
source: This resulted in virtually identical results for the HCP sample (r intra-hemisphere = 0.956, r inter-hemisphere = 0.843, Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is directly reported from the robustness analysis.

claim: Alignment improved the similarity to the pattern observed in HCP for the UKB sample (aligned r intra-hemisphere = 0.592, non-aligned r intra-hemisphere = 0.487, aligned r inter-hemisphere = 0.384, non-aligned r inter-hemisphere = 0.162).
source: At the same time, comparing unaligned and aligned gradients in the UKB sample, we found that the alignment improved the similarity to the pattern observed in HCP (aligned r intra-hemisphere = 0.592, non-aligned r intra-hemisphere = 0.487, aligned r inter-hemisphere = 0.384, non-aligned r inter-hemisphere = 0.162, Figure 2—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is directly reported from the robustness analysis.

claim: Along the principal gradient, the observed normalized asymmetric map was highly similar to the non-normalized map used in the main analyses for the intra-hemispheric (Pearson r=0.956) and inter-hemispheric (Pearson r=0.531) asymmetry patterns.
source: Indeed, along the principal gradient, the observed normalized asymmetric map was highly similar to the non-normalized map used in the main analyses for the intra-hemispheric (Pearson r=0.956) and inter-hemispheric (Pearson r=0.531) asymmetry patterns (Figure 2—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is directly reported from the robustness analysis.

claim: Using RR FC gradients as reference, all results were virtually identical (Pearson r intra G1=0.989, r intra G2=0.939, r intra G3=0.987, r inter G1=0.979, r inter G2=0.960, r inter G3=0.990, all P spin <0.001).
source: It suggested all results were virtually identical (Pearson r intra G1=0.989, r intra G2=0.939, r intra G3=0.987, r inter G1=0.979, r inter G2=0.960, r inter G3=0.990, all P spin <0.001).
evidence: This is directly reported from the robustness analysis.

claim: Regions belonging to the language network showed the strongest leftward preference along the principal gradient axis for intra-hemispheric asymmetry gradients.
source: For the intra-hemispheric asymmetry gradients, we found that regions belonging to the language network showed the strongest leftward preference along the principal gradient axis.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis and discussion of results.

claim: Ventral multimodal networks were closer to the transmodal apex of the principal gradient in the right hemisphere, relative to their homologues in the left hemisphere.
source: Conversely, ventral multimodal networks were closer to the transmodal apex of the principal gradient in the right hemisphere, relative to their homologues in the left hemisphere.
evidence: This is inferred from the data analysis results.

claim: Anterior lateral default mode subnetworks uniquely exhibit positive connectivity to the language network.
source: Anterior lateral default mode subnetworks have been shown to uniquely exhibit positive connectivity to the language network (Gordon et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The observed dissociation between language and control networks is in line with previous work suggesting an inverse pattern of language and attention between hemispheres.
source: The observed dissociation between language and control networks is also in line with previous work suggesting an inverse pattern of language and attention between hemispheres (Karolis et al., 2019; Zago et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and inference from current results.

claim: Brain structure including cortical thickness, surface area, and white matter connection are heritable.
source: Previous work indicated that brain structure including cortical thickness, surface area, and white matter connection (Kong et al., 2018; Sha et al., 2021; Zhong et al., 2021), as well as functional connectome organization (Colclough et al., 2017; Ge et al., 2017) are heritable.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Functional connectome organization is heritable.
source: Previous work indicated that brain structure including cortical thickness, surface area, and white matter connection (Kong et al., 2018; Sha et al., 2021; Zhong et al., 2021), as well as functional connectome organization (Colclough et al., 2017; Ge et al., 2017) are heritable.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Temporal language areas showed high heritability of cortical thickness asymmetry.
source: For example, previous work found that temporal language areas showed high heritability of cortical thickness asymmetry (Sha et al., 2021) and white matter connection asymmetry (Zhong et al., 2021) but frontal language areas did not.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Frontal language areas did not show high heritability of cortical thickness asymmetry or white matter connection asymmetry.
source: For example, previous work found that temporal language areas showed high heritability of cortical thickness asymmetry (Sha et al., 2021) and white matter connection asymmetry (Zhong et al., 2021) but frontal language areas did not.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Broca's area may mature after more posterior language regions in hierarchical fashion.
source: It is thus possible that Broca's area may mature after more posterior language regions in hierarchical fashion, which may be related to decreasing heritability in frontal language areas (i.e. more influenced by developmental and/or environmental factors).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from observed patterns.

claim: Asymmetric patterning of brain structure and function are largely determined prenatally and unaffected by preterm birth.
source: Recent work suggests that asymmetric patterning of brain structure and function are largely determined prenatally and unaffected by preterm birth (Williams et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In neonates, asymmetric patterns were largely observed in primary and unimodal areas, whereas association regions were largely symmetric.
source: In neonates, asymmetric patterns were largely observed in primary and unimodal areas, whereas association regions were largely symmetric.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Williams et al., 2021).

claim: Asymmetry in association regions may be more experience-dependent.
source: Thus, asymmetry in association regions may be more experience-dependent.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that association regions are symmetric in neonates.

claim: Functional asymmetry of within-hemispheric connectivity may be conserved across primates.
source: This indicates functional asymmetry of within-hemispheric connectivity may be conserved across primates.
evidence: This is inferred from the cross-species comparison showing similarity in intra-hemispheric asymmetry patterns.

claim: Regions involved in higher order cognitive functions in humans are particularly asymmetric.
source: These findings may support the notion that though asymmetry is a phenomenon existent across different primates, regions involved in higher order cognitive functions in humans are particularly asymmetric.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that language and frontoparietal networks show greater asymmetry in humans than macaques.

claim: Humans showed more leftward arcuate fasciculus volume and surface relative to macaques.
source: Previous work studying asymmetry in white matter structure in primates found that humans showed more leftward arcuate fasciculus volume and surface relative to macaques (Eichert et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The arcuate fasciculus is a white matter tract implicated in language functions by connecting Broca's and Wernicke's areas.
source: The arcuate fasciculus is a white matter tract implicated in language functions by connecting Broca's and Wernicke's areas (Geschwind, 1970).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Evolutionary modifications to the arcuate fasciculus in humans relative to other primates have been reported, possibly derived from auditory pathways.
source: Moreover, by comparing humans, macaques, and chimpanzees (Eichert et al., 2020), evolutionary modifications to this tract in humans relative to other primates have been reported, possibly derived from auditory pathways (Balezeau et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Leftward asymmetry of language areas has been observed in chimpanzees.
source: At the same time, other structural studies have also observed leftward asymmetry of language areas in chimpanzees, indicating that asymmetry of language-regions per se may not be a human-specific feature (Spocter et al., 2020; Xiang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: There are no significant differences of thickness and area asymmetry between humans and chimpanzees in superior temporal lobe.
source: Fittingly, there are no significant differences of thickness and area asymmetry between humans and chimpanzees in superior temporal lobe (Xiang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Temporal and occipital cortices showed local differences in asymmetry across species, and much more variability in humans relative to non-human primates.
source: Studying the endocranial shape of humans and non-human primates, temporal and occipital cortices showed local differences in asymmetry across species, and much more variability in humans relative to non-human primates (Neubauer et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Brain asymmetry is a phenomenon observed throughout mammals.
source: This suggests that whereas brain asymmetry is a phenomenon observed throughout mammals (Assaf et al., 2020), specific nuances may relate to species-specific behavioral and cognitive differences.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Intra-hemispheric asymmetry relates to association fibers.
source: Whereas intra-hemispheric asymmetry relates to association fibers, commissural fibers underlie inter-hemispheric connections (Tzourio-Mazoyer, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Commissural fibers underlie inter-hemispheric connections.
source: Whereas intra-hemispheric asymmetry relates to association fibers, commissural fibers underlie inter-hemispheric connections (Tzourio-Mazoyer, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: There is a trade-off within and across mammals of inter- and intra-hemispheric connectivity patterns to conserve the balance between gray and white-matter.
source: It has been suggested that there is a trade-off within and across mammals of inter- and intra-hemispheric connectivity patterns to conserve the balance between gray and white-matter (Assaf et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: There is a developmental trajectory from inter- to intra-hemispheric organization of functional brain connectivity, varying from unimodal to transmodal areas.
source: Secondly, previous research studying intra- and inter-hemispheric connectivity and associated asymmetry, has indicated a developmental trajectory from inter- to intra-hemispheric organization of functional brain connectivity, varying from unimodal to transmodal areas (Friederici et al., 2011; Szaflarski et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Task-based activations associated with language processing leaned leftward while task-based activations associated with executive functions leaned rightward in the intra-hemispheric pattern.
source: In line with our expectations based on the distribution of asymmetry within functional networks, we found that task-based activations associated with language processing leaned leftward while task-based activations associated with executive functions leaned rightward, specifically in the intra-hemispheric pattern.
evidence: This is supported by the functional decoding analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Lateralized functions supported by the brain's asymmetry have functional relevance, especially higher order cognitive functions such as language and executive control.
source: This suggests that lateralized functions supported by the brain's asymmetry have functional relevance (especially higher order cognitive functions such as language and executive control).
evidence: This is inferred from the functional decoding results.

claim: Asymmetry of individuals relates to variation in behavioral performance in semantic and visual recognition domains.
source: Indeed, related work has shown a direct link between asymmetry and semantic and visual recognition skills (Gonzalez Alam et al., 2022), suggesting that asymmetry of individuals relates to variation in behavioral performance in these domains (Gonzalez Alam et al., 2022; Gonzalez Alam et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Left hemispheric language lateralization is enabled throughout language development while right hemispheric language activation declines systematically with age.
source: Notably, left hemispheric language lateralization is enabled throughout language development while right hemispheric language activation declines systematically with age (Olulade et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.
